reasons: fact-check: score.evidence[0].note: The score for Shoulder Arms was composed by Charles Chaplin in 1959 (with Eric James as musical associate). Timothy Brock restored it for live performance in 2002 and created a reduced-orchestra version in 2004; he is not the composer. Describing it as 'a newly adapted musical score by composer Timothy Brock' misattributes authorship and implies Brock wrote original music for the 2026 restoration, when he restored and adapted Chaplin's pre-existing score. -> Credit the score to Charles Chaplin (composed 1959) and describe Brock's role as restoring/adapting Chaplin's score for the 2026 restoration, not composing it.

fact-check: editorial: The editorial says Chaplin 'hallucinates he is an oak tree.' Within the film's dream narrative the soldier deliberately dons a tree costume as a spy disguise to infiltrate German lines — he is not having a spontaneous hallucination that he is a tree. Additionally no source identifies the tree type as 'oak'; every contemporaneous and reference source describes it simply as 'a tree.' -> Change to 'disguises himself as a tree' and remove the species identification 'oak'.

fact-check: layers.story.evidence[0].note: States the play text 'was written in Belgium.' Maeterlinck moved to a villa in Grasse, in the south of France, in 1906, and Wikipedia's article on Maeterlinck explicitly states The Blue Bird was 'largely written in 1906' while he was living in Grasse, France — not Belgium. -> Change 'written in Belgium' to 'written in France' (specifically Grasse, in the south of France).

fact-check: layers.restorations.evidence[0].note: Claims the surviving nitrate print was 'sourced from the Cinémathèque Française.' No source found supports this. The cited source (silentfilmondvd.blogspot.com) makes no mention of the Cinémathèque Française; it states the print was 'preserved from decomposing nitrate elements by the George Eastman House (as part of the National Endowment for the Arts and the U.S. Parks Service's saving America's Treasures program)' — implying the print was already US-held. The filmcolors.org gallery for this film identifies the print source as the Library of Congress, not a French archive. -> Remove the Cinémathèque Française attribution. No accessible source places the surviving nitrate print at a French archive; the preservation was conducted by George Eastman House under a US federal program.

fact-check: editorial: Ernst Laemmle is listed as an additional uncredited director of the original 1925 silent film alongside Lon Chaney and Edward Sedgwick, but Laemmle's directorial work was on the 1929 sound reissue—he and Frank McCormick reshot nearly half the picture with synchronized sound in August 1929—not the original 1925 production. -> Remove Ernst Laemmle from the list of uncredited directors of the 1925 production. fact-check: editorial: 'Julius Jaenzon's cinematography pioneered double-exposure techniques' is factually wrong. Double exposure was already a well-established technique developed by Georges Méliès and others in the 1900s–1910s, and Sjöström/Jaenzon had themselves used it in Dödskyssen (1916). The film advanced and refined the technique to unusual complexity, but did not pioneer it. -> Replace 'pioneered' with 'advanced' or 'refined'; e.g. '…Julius Jaenzon's cinematography used multi-layered double-exposure techniques to depict the ghostly Death's carriage.'

fact-check: editorial: 'Victor Sjöström for SF Studios' is anachronistic. The production company in 1921 was Svensk Filmindustri (AB Svensk Filmindustri); it did not rebrand to SF Studios until 2016. -> Replace 'SF Studios' with 'Svensk Filmindustri'.
